changes: Rename 'stem-and-leaf plot' to 'stem plot', the term the VCE Mathematics Study Design uses.
Add that a display is chosen to show the shape, centre, spread and outliers of the data, as the new point's brief asks.
match.reason: The bank card covers the same display choices, but it uses the NSW term for stem plots and does not say that displays should show shape, centre, spread and outliers.

confirm.reason: The closest bank point, Displaying data, is about picking a display, including column graphs for categorical data, and never covers reading shape, centre, spread and outliers from a histogram, stem plot or dot plot, which is the heart of this point.

draft.title: Histograms, stem plots and dot plots
card: Dot plot
One dot for each value, stacked above a number line. It suits a small set of data with few different values, such as 20 quiz scores out of 10.
Stem plot
Each value is split into a stem (the leading digits) and a leaf (the last digit). 47 has stem 4 and leaf 7. It keeps every value and suits small to medium sets.
Histogram
Bars show how many values fall in each equal-width interval, and the bars touch. It suits large sets, but the individual values are lost.
All three show shape, centre, spread and outliers. An outlier is a value far from the rest, set apart by a gap in the display.
draft.remember: Dot and stem plots keep each value. A histogram groups values into intervals.

a.q: A stem plot has the row 3 | 2 5 5 8. Which values does this row show?
a.why: The stem 3 is the leading digit and each leaf is a last digit. So the row shows 32, 35, 35 and 38. Reading all the leaves as one number, or as separate values, ignores the stem.
a.clue: Put the stem in front of each leaf.

b.q: Ravi records the heights of 400 students in Geelong. Which display suits this large set best?
opts: A dot plot with one dot per student
A stem plot listing all 400 values
A segmented bar chart of the heights
b.why: With 400 measured values, grouping into intervals keeps the shape clear. A dot plot or stem plot would be very crowded, as each shows every value. A segmented bar chart is for categorical data, not heights.
b.clue: Which display groups values instead of showing each one?

problems.detail: The card defines an outlier as 'a value far from the rest, set apart by a gap in the display'. Outliers are defined formally in point 6 (beyond the fences, 1.5 IQRs past the quartiles), and a gap is neither necessary nor sufficient for that. Saying outliers can show up as values apart from the rest, without making the gap the definition, would avoid clashing with point 6.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and have one clear answer. The only issue is the card's gap-based definition of an outlier, which belongs to point 6 and does not match its fence rule.

a.q: A stem plot has the row 3 | 2 5 5 8. Which values does this row show?
a.why: The stem 3 is the leading digit and each leaf is a last digit, so the row shows 32, 35, 35 and 38. Each leaf is one value, so the repeated 5 means 35 appears twice. Writing the leaf first, or reading the stem as its own value, misreads the plot.
a.clue: Put the stem in front of each leaf, one value per leaf.
